notes.definition: Extinction is when there are no remaining individuals of a species still alive. Factors that may contribute to extinction include new predators, new diseases, new more successful competitors, changes to the environment over geological time and single catastrophic events.
explanation: A species becomes extinct when there are no individuals of that species left alive anywhere. Once a species is extinct it cannot come back, because there are no individuals left to reproduce. Extinction is a normal part of the history of life: the fossil record shows that most species that have ever lived are now extinct. You need to be able to describe the factors that may contribute to the extinction of a species.

New predators can cause extinction. If a predator arrives in a habitat where it did not live before, the prey species may not have evolved any way to escape or defend itself, so it is eaten faster than it can reproduce. Island species are especially at risk. For example, the dodo, a flightless bird on Mauritius, became extinct after humans arrived and hunted it, and animals they brought, such as rats and pigs, ate its eggs.

New diseases can also cause extinction. If a new pathogen arrives, the individuals of a species may have no resistance or immunity to it, so many of them die. If the population becomes very small, it may not recover. New, more successful competitors are another cause. A competitor that is better at getting the same resources, such as food, water, space or mates, may take so many of them that the original species cannot survive and reproduce in enough numbers.

Changes to the environment over geological time can cause extinction. For example, the climate may slowly become colder or drier, or sea levels may change, over thousands or millions of years. If a species cannot adapt, because natural selection does not produce suitable changes fast enough, it will die out. Species that reproduce slowly, have little genetic variation or live in only one small area are at greater risk.

A single catastrophic event can wipe out many species at once. Examples are massive volcanic eruptions and asteroid collisions. Scientists think that the dinosaurs became extinct about 66 million years ago after a large asteroid hit the Earth. Dust and gas thrown into the atmosphere would have blocked sunlight, lowering temperatures and reducing photosynthesis, so plants died and food chains collapsed.

Often several factors act together. A population already reduced by a new competitor may then be finished off by a disease or a change in climate. Today, human activities such as habitat destruction, hunting and pollution, and the introduction of species to new places, have increased the rate at which species are becoming extinct.
keyFacts: Extinction means there are no remaining individuals of a species still alive.
New predators can cause extinction if the prey has no way of escaping or defending itself.
New diseases can cause extinction if the species has no resistance or immunity.
New, more successful competitors can out-compete a species for food, water, space or mates.
Changes to the environment over geological time (such as climate change) can cause extinction if species cannot adapt quickly enough.
Single catastrophic events, such as massive volcanic eruptions or asteroid collisions, can cause many extinctions at once.
An asteroid collision is thought to have caused the extinction of the dinosaurs about 66 million years ago.
The fossil record shows that most species that have ever lived are now extinct.
Species with small populations, slow reproduction or little genetic variation are at greater risk.

keyTerms.definition: When there are no remaining individuals of a species still alive.
An animal that kills and eats other animals (its prey).
An organism that needs the same limited resources, such as food, space, water or mates, as another organism.
A microorganism that causes an infectious disease.
The very long timescale of Earth's history, measured in thousands to millions of years.
A sudden, very large event, such as a massive volcanic eruption or an asteroid collision, that changes conditions across large areas of Earth.
Differences in alleles between individuals in a population; more variation makes it more likely some individuals survive a change.

workedExamples.title: Calculating a percentage decrease in a population
workedExamples.question: A population of a rare frog fell from 2400 to 600 after a new fungal disease arrived. Calculate the percentage decrease.

workedExamples.title: Identifying the factor that caused an extinction
workedExamples.question: For each case, name the factor: (a) a bird on an island dies out after rats arrive and eat its eggs; (b) many species die out after a huge volcanic eruption; (c) a plant dies out as the climate slowly becomes drier over a million years.
steps: (a) The rats are a new predator of the eggs.
(b) A huge eruption is a single catastrophic event.
(c) Slow drying over a million years is a change to the environment over geological time.
workedExamples.answer: (a) New predator. (b) Single catastrophic event. (c) Change to the environment over geological time.

workedExamples.question: A population of 3200 animals halves every 3 years because of a new disease. Predict the population after 12 years if nothing changes.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a species is extinct when it becomes rare or disappears from one country.
misconceptions.right: In fact, a species is only extinct when there are no remaining individuals alive anywhere. Red squirrels have disappeared from much of England but are not extinct.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think extinction only happens because of humans.
misconceptions.right: In fact, extinctions have always happened because of new predators, diseases, competitors, environmental change and catastrophic events. Humans have increased the rate.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think animals can choose to adapt quickly when their environment changes.
misconceptions.right: In fact, adaptation happens by natural selection over many generations. If change is too fast, or there is too little variation, the species dies out.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a single factor always explains an extinction.
misconceptions.right: In fact, several factors often combine, for example competition reducing a population that is then hit by disease.

realWorld: The dodo on Mauritius became extinct in the 17th century after humans hunted it and introduced animals such as rats and pigs ate its eggs.
Red squirrels in Britain have declined because introduced grey squirrels out-compete them for food and carry squirrelpox virus, which kills red squirrels.
Conservation programmes such as captive breeding and protecting habitats aim to stop endangered species becoming extinct.
examTips: Learn the five factors: new predators, new diseases, new more successful competitors, environmental change over geological time, single catastrophic events.
Always explain how the factor leads to extinction, for example 'the prey has not evolved a way to escape, so it is eaten faster than it can reproduce'.
Give an example of a catastrophic event: massive volcanic eruption or asteroid collision.
For percentage decrease, divide the decrease by the original value, not the new value.
In longer answers, link extinction to natural selection: if no individuals have alleles that help them survive the change, none survive to reproduce.
summary: Extinction: no remaining individuals of a species still alive.
New predators and new diseases can kill individuals faster than they can reproduce.
New, more successful competitors can take the resources a species needs.
Environmental changes over geological time can be too fast for species to adapt.
Single catastrophic events, such as asteroid collisions, can cause many extinctions at once.

questions.question: What is meant by extinction?
options: A species has moved to a new habitat
There are no remaining individuals of a species still alive
A species has a very small population
A species is no longer found in one country
markScheme: 1 mark: there are no remaining individuals of a species still alive
questions.explanation: Extinction means none are left anywhere. A small population means the species is endangered, and disappearing from one country is local loss, not extinction.

questions.question: Which of these is a single catastrophic event that could cause extinction?
options: A new competitor arriving
Slow cooling of the climate over a million years
A new disease spreading
An asteroid collision
markScheme: 1 mark: an asteroid collision
questions.explanation: Catastrophic events are sudden and huge, such as asteroid collisions or massive volcanic eruptions. Slow cooling is a change over geological time, and competitors and disease are separate factors.

questions.question: Which of these could contribute to the extinction of a species?
options: A new predator arriving in its habitat
An increase in its food supply
Fewer diseases in its habitat
Fewer competitors for its food
markScheme: 1 mark: a new predator arriving in its habitat
questions.explanation: A new predator can kill individuals faster than they reproduce. The other three options would help the species survive.

questions.question: What do most scientists think caused the extinction of the dinosaurs about 66 million years ago?
options: Hunting by humans
A new predator
An asteroid collision
A new competitor
markScheme: 1 mark: an asteroid collision
questions.explanation: The evidence points to a large asteroid hitting the Earth. Humans did not exist 66 million years ago.

questions.question: Why might a new disease cause a species to become extinct?
options: The disease makes the species reproduce faster
Individuals have no resistance or immunity, so many die
The disease only affects predators of the species
The disease increases genetic variation
markScheme: 1 mark: individuals have no resistance or immunity, so many die
questions.explanation: A species that has never met a pathogen has had no chance to evolve resistance, so the disease can kill most individuals.

questions.question: Grey squirrels were introduced to Britain and are better than red squirrels at finding and eating some foods. Which factor that contributes to extinction does this describe?
options: A new predator
A catastrophic event
Environmental change over geological time
A new, more successful competitor
markScheme: 1 mark: a new, more successful competitor
questions.explanation: Grey squirrels compete with red squirrels for food; they do not eat red squirrels, so they are not predators. (They also carry squirrelpox, which is a disease factor.)

questions.question: Which is an example of a change to the environment over geological time?
options: The climate slowly becoming colder over millions of years
A forest fire lasting one week
A new species of fox arriving on an island
A hurricane hitting an island
markScheme: 1 mark: the climate slowly becoming colder over millions of years
questions.explanation: Geological time means thousands to millions of years. Fires and hurricanes are short events, and a new fox is a new predator.

questions.question: Why are species that live only on small islands often at high risk of extinction when a new predator arrives?
options: Island species reproduce faster than mainland species
Island species always have more genetic variation
They have not evolved ways to escape or defend themselves from that predator
Predators cannot reach islands
markScheme: 1 mark: they have not evolved ways to escape or defend themselves from that predator
questions.explanation: Island species often evolved without that predator, so they may have no defences (the dodo could not even fly). Island populations are also usually small, with limited variation.

questions.question: Why is a species with very little genetic variation more likely to become extinct when a new disease appears?
options: It reproduces more slowly
It is less likely that any individuals have alleles that help them survive the disease
It is more likely to be eaten by predators
It cannot catch diseases
markScheme: 1 mark: less likely that any individuals have alleles that help them survive
questions.explanation: Natural selection can only work if some individuals already carry useful alleles. With little variation, the disease may kill almost every individual.

questions.question: Which species is most at risk of extinction?
options: A bird with a large population spread across three continents that eats many types of food
A weed that grows in many countries and produces thousands of seeds each year
An insect with many generations each year and lots of genetic variation
A large mammal found on one island, with a small population, that eats only one type of plant
markScheme: 1 mark: the large mammal on one island with a small population that eats one type of plant
questions.explanation: A small population in one place with a specialised diet and (as a large mammal) slow reproduction is very vulnerable. A single disease, competitor or change to its food plant could wipe it out.

questions.question:
A new fungal disease arrived in the habitat of a population of frogs.
Table 1 shows the population before and after the disease arrived.
Calculate the percentage decrease in the population.
markScheme: 1 mark: decrease = 2400 − 600 = 1800
questions.explanation: Percentage decrease = decrease ÷ original × 100. Dividing by 600 instead of 2400 is a common mistake.

questions.question:
Rats were introduced to an island.
Table 1 shows information about the bird species on the island.
Calculate the percentage of bird species that became extinct.

headers: Number of bird species before rats were introduced
Number of bird species that became extinct

questions.explanation: 14 ÷ 40 = 0.35, and 0.35 × 100 = 35%. The rats acted as a new predator, especially of eggs and chicks.

questions.question:
A new predator has arrived in the habitat of a species of tortoise.
Table 1 shows information about the tortoise population.
Calculate how many years it will take for the species to become extinct if this rate continues.
questions.explanation: The population falls by the same number each year, so divide the starting population by the yearly fall: 1200 ÷ 150 = 8 years.

questions.question: Give two factors that may contribute to the extinction of a species.
markScheme: 1 mark each, any two: new predators; new diseases; new, more successful competitors; changes to the environment over geological time; single catastrophic events (e.g. volcanic eruption, asteroid collision)
questions.explanation: These are the factors listed in the specification. Habitat destruction and hunting by humans are also accepted in many mark schemes.

questions.question: Give one example of a single catastrophic event that could cause many species to become extinct.
markScheme: 1 mark: asteroid collision / massive volcanic eruption
questions.explanation: Both examples suddenly change conditions over very large areas, affecting many species at once.

questions.question: Name one resource that a new competitor might compete for.
markScheme: 1 mark: food / space / water / mates (accept light or mineral ions for plants)
questions.explanation: Animals compete for food, water, space and mates; plants compete for light, space, water and mineral ions.

questions.question: Explain how the arrival of a new predator could lead to the extinction of a prey species.
markScheme: 1 mark: the prey has not evolved ways to escape or defend itself from the new predator
1 mark: so individuals are eaten faster than they can reproduce, until none are left
questions.explanation: The key idea is that the prey is not adapted to that predator, so the death rate is greater than the birth rate.

questions.question: Explain why a change in the climate over thousands of years could cause a species to become extinct.
markScheme: 1 mark: the species may no longer be suited to the new conditions / its food or habitat may be lost
1 mark: if it cannot adapt (by natural selection) quickly enough, individuals do not survive to reproduce and the species dies out
questions.explanation: Even a slow change can be too fast for a species that reproduces slowly or has little variation.

questions.question: Explain how a new, more successful competitor could cause a species to become extinct.
markScheme: 1 mark: the competitor is better at getting the same resources (e.g. food, space, mates)
1 mark: so fewer of the original species survive and reproduce, and the population falls until none remain
questions.explanation: Competitors do not have to kill the other species: taking its resources is enough to stop it surviving and reproducing.

questions.question:
The dodo was a large, flightless bird found only on the island of Mauritius.
It became extinct within about 100 years of humans arriving. Humans hunted dodos and brought rats and pigs with them, which ate dodo eggs.
Suggest three reasons why the dodo became extinct.
markScheme: 1 mark: humans were a new predator that hunted dodos
1 mark: rats and pigs were new predators of eggs, so few young were produced
1 mark: it was flightless / had no defences against new predators / lived only on one island so had a small population (accept competition with pigs for food)
questions.explanation: Several factors acted together. The dodo had evolved with no ground predators, so it had no way to escape the new ones.

questions.question: Suggest why species that reproduce slowly, such as elephants and whales, are at greater risk of extinction than species that reproduce quickly.
markScheme: 1 mark: their populations take a long time to recover / losses are not replaced quickly
1 mark: fewer generations means natural selection / adaptation to change is slower
questions.explanation: A fast-breeding species can recover numbers quickly and adapt over many generations. A slow-breeding species cannot.

questions.question: Explain how a single asteroid collision could cause the extinction of many different species, including animals that were not killed by the impact itself.
markScheme: 1 mark: dust / debris thrown into the atmosphere blocks sunlight (and temperatures fall)
1 mark: less photosynthesis so plants / producers die
1 mark: animals that depend on plants (and their predators) lose their food source, so food chains collapse
questions.explanation: The effects of the impact spread through food chains. Animals far from the impact die because their food supply disappears.

questions.question: Explain how fossils provide evidence that many species have become extinct.
acceptedAnswers: fossils of organisms not alive today
remains of species no longer found
markScheme: 1 mark: fossils are found of organisms that are not alive anywhere today
1 mark: the rock layers show when they lived, and they are absent from younger layers, showing when they died out
questions.explanation: If a type of organism appears in older rock layers but is never found in younger layers or alive today, it has become extinct.

questions.question: State the type of evidence that shows dinosaurs once lived on Earth.
markScheme: 1 mark: fossils
questions.explanation: Dinosaurs are extinct, so the only evidence that they existed comes from fossils, such as bones and footprints.

questions.question: Describe the factors that may contribute to the extinction of a species.
markScheme: Indicative content: new predators, which the species has no defence against, so individuals are eaten faster than they reproduce; new diseases, to which the species has no resistance or immunity; new, more successful competitors for food, space, water or mates; changes to the environment over geological time, e.g. climate change, too fast for the species to adapt; single catastrophic events, e.g. massive volcanic eruptions or asteroid collisions; examples such as the dodo or dinosaurs.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least three factors described, with explanation of how they lead to extinction.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): factors listed with little or no explanation.
questions.explanation: For the top level, say how each factor causes deaths or stops reproduction, not just its name.

questions.question:
Red squirrels are native to Britain. Grey squirrels were introduced from North America in the 19th century.
Table 1 compares the two species.
Explain why red squirrel populations have declined in most of England.
Suggest why red squirrels could become extinct in Britain.

rows: Carry the virus but are rarely harmed

markScheme: Indicative content: grey squirrels are a new, more successful competitor; they compete with red squirrels for the same food (e.g. acorns, nuts) and space; greys digest acorns more efficiently so get more energy from the same food; fewer red squirrels get enough food to survive and reproduce; squirrelpox is a new disease for red squirrels; red squirrels have no resistance or immunity, so most infected reds die; greys carry the virus without being harmed, so they spread it to new areas; the combination of competition and disease means red death rate exceeds birth rate; red populations are now small and isolated (e.g. in Scotland, islands); small populations have less genetic variation and could be wiped out by a disease outbreak or other change; if all remaining populations die out there will be no red squirrels in Britain (though the species is not extinct worldwide unless all populations die).
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed explanation using both competition and disease, clearly linked to survival and reproduction, with a reasoned suggestion about extinction risk.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explanation of competition or disease in detail, or both with less detail.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, e.g. 'grey squirrels took over' or 'they caught a disease', with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Identify both factors from the specification in the context: a new, more successful competitor and a new disease. Then explain the effect on survival and reproduction. Note that losing red squirrels from Britain would be local, not global, extinction.

questions.question:
A species of lizard lives only on one small island.
Table 1 shows information about the lizard species.
Scientists predict that the island's climate will become hotter and drier over the next 100 years.
Evaluate the risk that this lizard species will become extinct.
markScheme: Indicative content. Factors increasing risk: small population (300) so little genetic variation, so fewer individuals likely to have alleles suited to new conditions; found in only one place, so one event (e.g. disease, storm, new predator) could affect all individuals; relies on one food source, so if the insect declines in hot, dry conditions the lizard loses its food; climate change over 100 years may be too fast for adaptation by natural selection, especially if lizards reproduce slowly. Factors reducing risk: lizards may already tolerate heat; 100 years is many lizard generations so some adaptation possible; the insect may survive the change; conservation action (e.g. captive breeding) could help. Conclusion: overall risk is high.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): considers several factors that affect the risk, linked to the information given, with a justified conclusion.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant points with little evaluation or no conclusion.
questions.explanation: Use each piece of information in the question (population size, one island, one food, climate change) and finish with a judgement. Mentioning a point that reduces the risk shows evaluation.
